sources.title: Water Dechlorinator: How It Works and How Much to Use in Aquariums
Hướng Dẫn Với Quy Trình Thay Nước Hồ Cá Đúng Chuẩn Không Gây Sốc Cho Cá
Bao lâu thay nước bể cá 1 lần giúp bể cá sạch mọi cặn bẩn

facts.fact: Name for the term: "thay nước"
Name for the term: "thay nước định kỳ"
Name for the term: "water change"
Rising ammonia or nitrite levels can be controlled with frequent water changes.
Regular water changes are part of routine preventive care, with a change listed every 2 weeks in the maintenance schedule.
How much water to change depends on how heavily the tank is stocked.
Small tanks such as bowls may need more frequent changes, perhaps as much as 50% per week.
Tap water used in water changes puts back the carbonate and bicarbonate that buffer pH, which nitrifying bacteria use up.
Distilled and reverse osmosis water contain no carbonate or bicarbonate, so they do not restore alkalinity. The magazine does not recommend them for beginners' freshwater tanks.

Old tank syndrome: as alkalinity runs out, pH drops and ammonia shifts to less toxic ammonium. A water change raises pH again, turning it back into toxic ammonia, so fish can die soon after the change.
To keep nutrients and alkalinity under control, start with at least a 20 percent water change once a month.
If tap water is low in alkalinity, crushed coral or aragonite sand can add to it.
Large, frequent water changes are advised during a mycobacteriosis outbreak.
Dechlorinate any new water before it goes into the aquarium.
Stir the top of the substrate to release trapped waste, use a gravel vacuum while draining, and remove the debris you disturb.
Test pH, ammonia, nitrite and nitrate as part of routine maintenance.
Shop procedure step 1: turn off the pump, heater and lights.
Shop procedure step 2: scrape algae off the glass and lightly rinse dirty decorations.
Shop procedure step 3: siphon waste from the substrate one area at a time. Keep fish away from the intake, and do not drain the tank or let mature bio-media dry out.
Shop procedure step 4: rinse filter floss in old tank water so the beneficial bacteria survive.
Shop procedure step 5: add new water slowly, never pouring it straight onto the fish, and bring the temperature into line gradually.
Change about 20–30% of the water each time and keep at least 70% of the old water.
Tank temperature should change by no more than 0.5°C per hour.
For planted tanks, change 30–50% of the water per change, and never more than 50% at once.
Pour new water in gently so the substrate is not stirred up, then test ammonia, nitrite and nitrate afterwards.
Do not wash the container used for new water with soap, because the residue harms fish.
Chlorine evaporates: letting tap water stand for 1–5 days works if you are sure it holds only chlorine. Aerating with an air stone for 12–24 hours, or boiling for 15–20 minutes, is faster.
Aging tap water does not remove chloramine. Aquarium Co-Op says chloramine must be neutralized with dechlorinator.
City water contains chlorine or chloramine, both toxic to fish and to the tank's beneficial bacteria.
Aquarium Co-Op Easy Dechlorinator dose: 1 ml per 10 gallons of new water (3 ml for a 30-gallon change). For small tanks, use 2 drops per gallon.
Aquarium Co-Op doses dechlorinator for the volume of new water being added, not for the whole tank.
Dechlorinator neutralizes chlorine in about 2–5 minutes.
Easy Dechlorinator can be dosed at up to 5 times the normal amount within 24 hours for high chloramine or nitrite.
Overdosing dechlorinator lowers dissolved oxygen. After a heavy dose, run an air stone for 3–4 hours.
Changing water at dawn, when oxygen in planted tanks is lowest, is riskier because dechlorinator uses up oxygen as it works.
Some conditioners also bind ammonia for up to 24 hours, for example Easy Dechlorinator, Fritz Complete, Seachem Prime and Kordon AmQuel.
To remove chlorine without a conditioner, aerate strongly for 1–2 hours or leave the water outdoors in sunlight for 24 hours.
If tap water must be used at once, sodium thiosulfate ("Thiosunfat") can neutralize the chlorine.
Changing 100% of the water destroys the tank's stable bacteria and shocks fish, which can lead to lethargy or mass deaths.
Using untreated tap water can cause fish deaths with no obvious cause.
Changing water too often disrupts the filter bacteria and causes rapid swings in temperature and pH.
Never let water from a fish transport bag into the aquarium.
Signs of stress after moving or changing water include colour change, low activity, refusing food and red eyes.
A Vietnamese shop warns that tap water ("nước máy") usually contains chlorine that is extremely toxic to fish, so it must never be used untreated.
A Vietnamese shop advises using rainwater ("nước mưa") only after the season's first 3–4 rains, which are usually polluted.
A Vietnamese shop says well water ("nước giếng khoan") should be checked for dissolved oxygen (above 3 ppm) and pH (about 6–7).
A Vietnamese shop suggests running the tap for about 5 minutes before collecting water and storing it in a cool, airy spot.
